title: Nechemiah HaAmsoni (tanna)
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: He was a student of Rabbi Akiva. As in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot ch. 9 halakha 5 and Sotah ch. 5 halakha 5, they said that he served Rabbi Akiva for twenty-two years and learned from him that 'et' and 'gam' are amplifications, while 'akh' and 'rak' are limitations. He said to him: 'You shall fear the Lord your God' (et Hashem) — what does this include? He answered: Him and His Torah.

And we find in Pesachim 22b, Kiddushin 57, Bava Kamma 41, and Bekhorot 6a: Shimon HaAmsoni, and some say Nehemiah HaAmsoni, would expound every 'et' in the Torah; when he reached 'You shall fear the Lord your God (et Hashem)' he withdrew. His students said to him: Rabbi, what will be with all the 'etim' you expounded? He said to them: Just as I received reward for the expounding, so I receive reward for the withdrawing — until Rabbi Akiva came and expounded, etc. Hyman infers from this that he was before Rabbi Akiva.

Hyman writes that he found in Dikdukei Soferim that it cites a manuscript in which the words “His disciples said to him: Rabbi…” are absent. He argues that, if so, this resolves the Bavli and the Yerushalmi: that he truly received all this from his teacher Rabbi Akiva, and only 'et Hashem' he did not know how to expound until he finally heard it from Rabbi Akiva, his teacher.

notes.text: Hyman’s manuscript report omits the connected address “His disciples said to him: Rabbi…”. He proposes reconciling the Bavli and Yerushalmi through it. The Yerushalmi’s “Him and His Torah” is retained without harmonizing it to the Bavli.

The inspected Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 9:5 directly names Nechemiah Eimosoni, twenty-two years serving Akiva, and “Him and His Torah.” Pesachim 22b instead retains the disciples’ address and Akiva’s later arrival. These accounts are not harmonized. The exact manuscript omission reported through Dikdukei Soferim remains Hyman’s report and the reconciliation remains his inference.
